# Why DFS after BFS

BFS is about layers. It is the right mental model for shortest paths in
unweighted graphs.

DFS is about going deep, finishing a branch, and coming back with information.
That makes it the natural tool for:

```text
tree subtree sizes
parent and child relationships
entry/exit reasoning
cycle detection
postorder dynamic programming on trees
```

This section does not assume you already know DFS. It teaches the traversal,
the state variables, and the exact invariants used in the local exercises.

# Recognition

Look for these statement signals:

| Statement signal | Likely DFS idea |
|---|---|
| rooted tree, descendants, subtree | DFS with parent and postorder |
| "does this graph contain a cycle?" | DFS with parent/colors |
| need to process children before parent | DFS postorder |
| connected component traversal, no shortest path | BFS or DFS both work |
| dependency graph has impossible circular dependency | directed DFS colors |

BFS and DFS often visit the same set of vertices. The difference is the order
and what that order makes easy.

# Vocabulary

## Depth-first search

Depth-first search starts from a vertex, chooses an unvisited neighbor, goes as
deep as possible, and only then backs up.

For this graph:

```text
1 -- 2 -- 4
|    |
3    5
```

one possible DFS from `1` is:

```text
enter 1
  enter 2
    enter 4
    exit 4
    enter 5
    exit 5
  exit 2
  enter 3
  exit 3
exit 1
```

The exact order depends on adjacency-list order. Correctness should not depend
on one accidental ordering unless the problem explicitly asks for it.

## Parent

When DFS moves from `u` to an unseen neighbor `v`, we can record:

```text
parent[v] = u
```

In an undirected graph, `parent` prevents us from immediately treating the edge
back to the previous vertex as a cycle.

## Preorder and postorder

DFS has two important moments for each vertex:

```text
preorder:  when we first enter the vertex
postorder: after all children have been processed
```

Subtree sizes need postorder:

```text
size[u] = 1 + sum(size[child] for child of u)
```

You cannot finish `size[u]` until the child sizes are known.

# Recursive DFS primer

The most direct DFS is recursive:

```cpp
void dfs(int u, int p) {
    parent[u] = p;
    for (int v : adj[u]) {
        if (v == p) continue;
        dfs(v, u);
    }
}
```

Python:

```python
def dfs(u, p):
    parent[u] = p
    for v in adj[u]:
        if v == p:
            continue
        dfs(v, u)
```

This mirrors the definition. The function call stack remembers where to return
after a child finishes.

Contest warning: recursive DFS can overflow when the graph is a long chain of
`200000` vertices. C++ may stack overflow. Python needs `sys.setrecursionlimit`,
and even then recursion can be fragile. This course uses iterative solutions in
the reference code when depth can be large.

# Iterative DFS primer

An explicit stack can simulate recursive DFS.

For reachability:

```text
push start
mark start

while stack not empty:
    u = pop
    for v in adj[u]:
        if v is unseen:
            mark v
            push v
```

This visits the component, but it does not directly give postorder. For
postorder, use one of two patterns.

## Pattern 1: record order, then reverse it

This is enough on a tree:

```text
parent[root] = root
stack = [root]
order = []

while stack not empty:
    u = pop
    append u to order
    for v in adj[u]:
        if v == parent[u]: continue
        parent[v] = u
        push v

for u in reversed(order):
    add size[u] to size[parent[u]]
```

Because every child is pushed after its parent is recorded, reversing the
discovery order processes descendants before ancestors.

## Pattern 2: stack frames with next-neighbor index

This more closely simulates recursion and is useful for directed cycle
detection:

```text
stack contains (u, next_index_to_scan)

while stack not empty:
    u, i = top frame
    if i == number of neighbors:
        finish u
        pop frame
    else:
        scan neighbor adj[u][i]
        increment top frame's index
```

This lets us know whether a vertex is currently active in the DFS stack.

# Worked example 1: subtree sizes

Tree rooted at `1`:

```text
        1
      /   \
     2     3
    / \     \
   4   5     6
              \
               7
```

Leaves have subtree size `1`:

```text
size[4] = 1
size[5] = 1
size[7] = 1
```

Then:

```text
size[6] = 1 + size[7] = 2
size[2] = 1 + size[4] + size[5] = 3
size[3] = 1 + size[6] = 3
size[1] = 1 + size[2] + size[3] = 7
```

The important part is the direction of computation:

```text
children first, parent last
```

# Worked example 2: undirected cycle detection

Graph:

```text
1 -- 2 -- 3
|         |
+---------+
```

DFS:

```text
enter 1, parent none
enter 2, parent 1
enter 3, parent 2
see neighbor 1
```

At vertex `3`, neighbor `1` is already seen and is not `parent[3]`. That means
there is another route back to an earlier vertex:

```text
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1
```

So the graph has a cycle.

In an undirected graph, seeing the parent is normal:

```text
2 sees neighbor 1, but 1 is parent[2], so ignore it
```

# Worked example 3: directed cycle detection

Directed graph:

```text
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4
     ^         |
     +---------+
```

DFS colors:

```text
0 = unvisited
1 = currently active in this DFS stack
2 = completely finished
```

Trace:

```text
enter 1: color[1] = 1
enter 2: color[2] = 1
enter 3: color[3] = 1
enter 4: color[4] = 1
4 sees 2, and color[2] = 1
```

An edge to an active vertex is a back edge. It forms a directed cycle.

An edge to a finished vertex is different:

```text
u -> v and color[v] = 2
```

That edge does not prove a cycle, because `v` is not an ancestor on the current
DFS path.

# DFS colors

For directed cycle detection, use three states:

| Color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | never entered |
| 1 | entered but not finished; active on DFS stack |
| 2 | finished; all outgoing edges already checked |

Cycle rule:

```text
During DFS, if we inspect edge u -> v and color[v] == 1,
then a directed cycle exists.
```

Why the same color trick is not needed for undirected simple graphs:

```text
undirected cycle detection only needs seen[v] and parent skipping
```

# Components and disconnected graphs

Many graph inputs are disconnected. DFS from vertex `1` may not see everything.

The standard outer loop is:

```text
for start in all vertices:
    if start is unvisited:
        start a new DFS
```

This matters for cycle detection:

```text
one component may be acyclic
another component may contain the cycle
```

# Complexity

With adjacency lists:

```text
Time:  O(V + E)
Memory: O(V + E)
```

Each vertex is entered a constant number of times, and each adjacency-list item
is inspected a constant number of times.

For a tree:

```text
E = V - 1
Time: O(V)
```

# Implementation notes

## C++

Use adjacency lists:

```cpp
vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
```

For iterative DFS stacks:

```cpp
vector<int> st;
vector<pair<int,int>> frames;
```

Use `vector<char>` for Boolean or color arrays:

```cpp
vector<char> color(n, 0);
```

## Python

Use lists as stacks:

```python
stack = [start]
u = stack.pop()
stack.append(v)
```

This is efficient at the end of the list. Do not use `pop(0)` for stacks or
queues.

For large input:

```python
data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
```

# Local exercises

## A. Subtree Sizes

Use DFS to root the tree at `1`, then compute:

```text
subtree[u] = 1 + sum(subtree[child])
```

The reference solution uses discovery order reversed to get postorder.

## B. Undirected Cycle

Use DFS over every component. For each edge from `u` to `v`:

```text
if v == parent[u]: ignore it
else if v is already seen: cycle exists
else visit v with parent u
```

The input is simple, so there are no parallel-edge corner cases.

## C. Directed Cycle

Use DFS colors:

```text
0 unvisited
1 active
2 finished
```

An edge to color `1` means `CYCLIC`.

# Submission checklist

Before submitting:

```text
Did I run DFS from every component when the graph may be disconnected?
Did I store undirected edges both ways?
Did I skip only the parent edge in undirected cycle detection?
For directed graphs, did I distinguish active and finished vertices?
For subtree sizes, did I process children before parents?
Did I avoid recursive depth issues on large chains?
```
